content: Among the 300 pregnant women sampled, 200 are young pregnant women. Sampling would then continue exclusively among young pregnant women until an additional 100 young pregnant women are included. This method is more complex than simple inflation, as oversampling requires calculating and applying two distinct sample sizes to two different populations. This approach requires separate analyses. For example, the overall prevalence would be calculated for all eligible pregnant women aged 15–49 years using the first 300 women sampled, excluding the additional 100 young pregnant women. Prevalence among young pregnant women would then be calculated separately using the 200 young pregnant women from the initial sample and the additional 100 young pregnant women. Statistical modeling of trends in HIV prevalence among pregnant women served by sentinel surveillance sites involves simplified mathematical representations of hypotheses about key factors influencing or predicting HIV prevalence. These models are essential as they filter out random variations to identify significant effects on HIV prevalence. They allow for hypothesis testing against data evidence, adjustment of estimates for covariate effects, and data-driven predictions of new observations. Prevalence proportions are confined to the interval [0,1], and the logit transformation is commonly used to model factors affecting prevalence and analyze trends. Linear trends on the logit scale correspond to curvilinear trends on the prevalence scale, and trend analyses can be implemented using variations of logistic regression. The simplest methods use prevalence estimates from each surveillance round. If sampling variances are approximately equal, a mixed-effects linear regression model can be applied to logit-transformed prevalence data. This model includes fixed effects for time and random effects for site-specific variations. When sampling variances differ, weighting by the reciprocals of the variances can be used. However, this model assumes serial independence, meaning prevalence during one surveillance round is not influenced by the previous round. While this assumption may not always hold, it is often the only viable option when few rounds of surveillance data are available. The model provides site-specific intercepts and slopes on the logit scale, as well as among-site median-profile intercepts and slopes. Inferences about trends are based on confidence intervals for these parameters. Statistical software such as SAS, Stata, and R can be used to fit this model. Sentinel surveillance data collection forms typically include sociodemographic information (e.g., age, marital status, gravidity), HIV status at booking, antiretroviral therapy (ART) status, HIV testing information, and syphilis testing and treatment details. These forms are designed to capture comprehensive data for monitoring HIV and syphilis prevalence and treatment outcomes among pregnant women. Guidelines for conducting HIV surveillance emphasize the importance of using routine program data, ensuring data quality, and adhering to ethical principles. Statistical models and tools are critical for analyzing trends, making predictions, and informing public health strategies. These guidelines also highlight the need for standardized data collection, quality assurance, and confidentiality in HIV surveillance programs.
